Villelongue
veel-LOHNG
n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Aude of Languedoc, affiliated in the mid twelfth century; now a ruin in private hands)
Old French ville longue, the long settlement or farm, from Latin villa, a country estate, and longa, long.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Villelongue stands in the Aude, south-west of Carcassonne, a Cistercian house in the filiation of Bonnefont that grew from a small twelfth-century foundation into a modest abbey and then declined slowly through the wars of the later Middle Ages. Its church is roofless; what remains of the cloister and chapter house is in private hands. It is one of the many houses whose history is simply a long diminishment — no scandal, no suppression, no dramatic end, only centuries of fewer monks and smaller harvests until the buildings outnumbered the brethren. That ordinary trajectory deserves naming, because Scripture speaks a great deal about endurance and almost nothing about institutional survival. “For ye have need of patience, that, after ye have done the will of God, ye might receive the promise” (Heb 10:36) locates the promise beyond the doing; and the example offered is a man, not a foundation: “Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy” (Jam 5:11). A house that shrank for four hundred years is not a failure in that light; it simply was never the thing that was promised to last.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines villa as a country seat or farm house, and in Italy a country residence; ruin as the remains of a decayed or demolished structure; and patience as the suffering of afflictions with a calm, unruffled temper.

expand to see more

VILLA, n. A country seat or residence; originally, a farm or country house with its appendages.

RUIN, n. The remains of a decayed or demolished city, house or other work of men; destruction; fall; overthrow.

PATIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity, provocation or other evil, with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring or fretfulness.

DECLINE, v.i. To lean downward; to tend or draw toward a close; to fail; to sink; to decay.

ENDURE, v.i. To last; to continue in the same state without perishing; to remain; to abide.

Key Scripture

Heb 10:36 — "For ye have need of patience, that, after ye have done the will of God, ye might receive the promise."

Jam 5:11 — "Behold, we count them happy which endure. Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy."

Psa 102:26 — "They shall perish, but thou shalt endure: yea, all of them shall wax old like a garment; as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed:"

Mat 24:13 — "But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved."

Modern Corruption

A Languedoc Cistercian house whose history is a long diminishment: no scandal and no suppression, only four centuries of fewer monks.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that endurance is promised to persons and not to institutions. “But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved” (Mat 24:13) is singular; nothing in Scripture guarantees the continuance of a house, a denomination or a ministry.

The live comfort, and it is a real one, is that decline is not necessarily judgment. “They shall perish, but thou shalt endure: yea, all of them shall wax old like a garment” (Psa 102:26) treats the wearing out of made things as the ordinary order of creation. A congregation that is shrinking should ask whether it is faithful before it assumes it is cursed, and ask whether it is faithful before it assumes it is fine.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin villa longa, the long farm; Greek hupomone (G5281), patient endurance; Greek makrothumia (G3115), longsuffering; Hebrew qavah (H6960), to wait; Greek meno (G3306), to abide.

expand to see more

Latin villa longa — the long farm or settlement; a plain agricultural name, as Cistercian names usually are.

Greek hupomone (G5281) — endurance, a remaining under; “For ye have need of patience” (Heb 10:36).

Greek makrothumia (G3115) — longsuffering, long of temper; the companion virtue.

Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, remain; the verb of what lasts.

Hebrew qavah (H6960) — to wait, to look for with expectation; the Old Testament's patience.

Usage

"“that, after ye have done the will of God, ye might receive the promise” (Heb 10:36) — the promise is not the building."

"“Behold, we count them happy which endure” (Jam 5:11) — said of persons."

"“all of them shall wax old like a garment” (Psa 102:26) — the ordinary fate of made things."
